my take on recent university history (take it or leave it):

The Western university system greatly expanded after WWII. The thought was that there cannot afford to be a WWIII (duck-and-cover). University education would allow people to gain enough intellectual prowess that they would see their lives as having worth beyond mere cannon fodder on a foreign battlefield, and so it would be expected that young educated Westerners would vehemently refuse to participate in war.

However, no measures were put in place to stop students from becoming egotistical and believing their intellectual insights as a form of superiority

Next, the increased universities required expanded faculties to serve the massive student base. Philosophical structuralism which had worked during the age of Modernism unfortunately produces a terminus for relevant intellectual insight. Once you have a usable structuralist schema to explain phenomena you don't need thousands of researchers pushing discovery in that field. Even if you can still unveil information from that field, scholars will simply be retrofitting the established schema and not doing any work that distinguishes them as scholars. Thus they will be non-competitive in the academy.

And so, in the 1950s, the new generation of soft sciences faculty embraced the turn to hermeneutics and post-structuralist philosophy. This is where affect theory originates and where the current feminist ideology was spawned. Derrida, Bourdieu, Baudrillard, and other post-structuralists urged us to not trust in what we know and to not strive to prove a good or beautiful ideal. They preached that we have a "hermeneutic of suspicion" about everything (this is the essence of post-structuralism).

In turning to post-structuralism, new directions for soft science research opened up. When your "feelings" about a phenomenon count and are legitimated, you can now build an entire career around those feelings.

Now this is just one thread in the history... dealing mostly with the socio-cultural.

However, there is also the economic and industrial considerations.

So, the university system was expanded to deter Western nations from supporting international wars. However, the 1968 student protests made it obvious that educating young people and then not giving them jobs that challenged them intellectually only leads to disruptive agitation, revolutionary spirit, and mass protest.

And so Reaganism provided a viable solution (and this was an economic agenda being pushed even back in the 50s but not picking up full steam until the 80s). The mandate of Reaganomics was to export manufacturing-based industry to the "developing" world. The West would focus entirely on service-based industry.

Service-based industry provides work that requires a higher education than manufacturing. Of course, the universities prior to the 50s were too difficult for everyday people to graduate and so the bar for passing and getting a bachelor's degree started to be lowered. The lowering of the bar became more radical as the West fully shifted to service-based work.

A problem we have is that Westerners with BAs often believe that they are more intellectually capable than they actually are. They consider the age-old reputation of universities to validate their intellect while ignoring that their BA during the post-modern era is equivalent to having graduated high school in the first half of the 20th century.
